claims.claim: Interest on the national debt now costs far more than it used to.
claims.test: Supported if central government debt interest as a share of GDP in 2025-26 is more than 1 percentage point above its 1999-00 to 2019-20 average; partly if above the average by less; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: Central government debt interest is £108.9bn in 2025-26: 3.5% of GDP and 8.8% of all government receipts, against 2.0% of GDP on average from 1999-00 to 2019-20 (£39.3bn in 2019-20). The OBR forecasts £137.1bn by 2030-31.

series.name: Debt interest, % of GDP

notes: Net of the Bank of England's Asset Purchase Facility, as the OBR defines it.
Departmental figures are total managed expenditure for 2025-26 from the Treasury's PESA tables, shown for scale only.

claims.claim: The national debt is at levels not seen since the 1960s.
claims.test: Supported if the last year before 2025-26 in which public sector net debt was as high a share of GDP as today was before 1970; partly if before 1990; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: Public sector net debt is 93.3% of GDP in 2025-26. It has been at or above this level continuously since 2023-24; before that it was last this high in 2021-22 (the peak was 251.7% in 1946-47); the OBR forecasts 95.1% by 2030-31.

series.name: Public sector net debt, % of GDP

notes: The long series is the OBR's 'public finances since 1900' (debt as a share of GDP, including the Bank of England).

claims.claim: Government borrowing is out of control.
claims.test: Supported if net borrowing as a share of GDP in 2025-26 is more than 2 percentage points above its 1999-00 to 2019-20 average; partly if above the average by less; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: Government borrowing is 4.4% of GDP in 2025-26 (£134bn), against 2.6% in 2019-20 and an average of 3.9% from 1999-00 to 2019-20; the OBR forecasts 1.6% by 2030-31.

series.name: Public sector net borrowing, % of GDP

claims.claim: The state is bigger than it has ever been.
claims.test: Supported if total government spending as a share of GDP in 2025-26 is higher than in every earlier year outside the two world wars and 2020-21; partly if within 1 percentage point of the highest; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: Total government spending is 44.5% of GDP in 2025-26; 39.2% in 2019-20 and 46.0% in 2009-10. The highest in peacetime outside the pandemic was 46.5% in 1975-76; spending was higher than today in 5 earlier years (most recently 2010-11).

series.name: Total managed expenditure, % of GDP

notes: Excludes the war years 1914-1920 and 1939-1946 and 2020-21 from the 'highest outside crisis years' comparison (the list is in the test).

claims.claim: Taxes are at record levels.
claims.test: Supported if government receipts as a share of GDP in 2025-26 are higher than in every earlier year since 1946-47; partly if within 1 percentage point of the highest; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: Government receipts (taxes and other income) are 40.1% of GDP in 2025-26, against 36.6% in 2019-20. The post-war peak was 43.3% in 1949-50; receipts were higher in 10 earlier years (most recently 1982-83). The OBR forecasts 42.7% by 2030-31.

series.name: Public sector current receipts, % of GDP

notes: Receipts include taxes, interest and dividends, and the operating surplus of public bodies, not only taxes.

claims.claim: Asylum claims are at record levels.
claims.test: Supported if the people claiming asylum in the latest 12 months are at least as many as in any calendar year since 2010; partly if within 25% of the record; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: 85,891 people claimed asylum in the year ending June 2026 (108,585 a year earlier). The record is 104,764 in calendar 2024, so the latest year is 18% below it, and 1.9 times the 2019 level (45,537).

series.name: People claiming asylum, main applicants and dependants

notes: People, including dependants, by date of claim. The latest point is a rolling year, the others are calendar years.

claims.claim: Most people claiming asylum arrive on small boats.
claims.test: Supported if more than 50% of people claiming asylum in the latest 12 months arrived by small boat; partly if between 30% and 50%; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: 33,949 of the 85,891 people who claimed asylum in the year ending June 2026 had arrived by small boat: 39.5%. The share peaked at 45% and was 1% in 2018.

series.name: Share of asylum claimants who arrived by small boat, %

notes: Route is the one recorded before the claim. About 8% of claimants have a route recorded as 'Other'.

claims.claim: Most people claiming asylum entered the country illegally.
claims.test: Supported if more than 50% of people claiming asylum in the latest 12 months came by a route the Home Office classes as illegal entry (small boat, clandestine, entered without relevant documents); partly if between 30% and 50%.
claims.headline: 44,297 of 85,891 asylum claimants (51.6%) came by a route the Home Office classes as illegal entry (small boat 33,949, clandestine 6,999, without relevant documents 3,349); 55.9% if the 6,595 with no recorded route are left out. The rest (34,999) held a visa or other permission to be here.

notes: Claiming asylum is lawful whatever the route of entry; 'illegal entry' here is the Home Office's classification of how the person arrived.

claims.claim: Lots of people claim asylum after arriving legally on a visa.
claims.test: A factual question: the number and share of people claiming asylum in the latest 12 months who held a work, study, visitor or other visa. No threshold; the numbers are the answer.
claims.headline: 34,999 people (40.7%) who claimed asylum in the year ending June 2026 already held a visa or other leave: 14,151 work, 9,442 study, 6,392 visitor, 5,014 other. That share was 30% in 2018 and 39% in 2025.

series.name: Share of asylum claimants who held a visa or other leave, %

claims.claim: Small boat crossings keep rising.
claims.test: Supported if small boat arrivals in the latest 12 months are more than 10% above the previous 12 months; partly if within 10% either way; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: 33,374 people arrived by small boat in the year ending June 2026, 23% fewer than the 43,309 in the year before. The record year is 2022 with 45,774.

series.name: Small boat arrivals per calendar year

notes: Top nationalities of small boat arrivals in the latest year are shown as bars (people).

claims.claim: Hardly anyone refused asylum is ever removed.
claims.test: Using everyone who claimed in 2018 to 2022: returns recorded per 100 people finally refused after appeal. Supported if under 25; partly if 25 to 50; not supported if 50 or more.
claims.headline: Of people who claimed asylum in 2018 to 2022, 42,826 were finally refused (after any appeal) and 20,111 have a recorded return (6,691 enforced): about 47 returns for every 100 refusals.

notes: Returns are counted for the whole claim cohort, so some are people who were later granted or withdrew. The ratio is an indicator, not the exact share of refused people removed.
A refused person may also have left without a recorded return.

claims.claim: Enforced removals are rising.
claims.test: Supported if enforced returns in the latest 12 months are more than 10% above the previous 12 months; partly if within 10% either way; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: 9,669 people were removed by enforcement in the year ending June 2026 (+7% on the 9,077 a year before), plus 30,936 voluntary returns. The highest calendar year since 2010 is 2012 with 15,134 enforced returns.

series.name: Enforced returns per calendar year, all nationalities

notes: Enforced returns include foreign national offenders and people who were not asylum seekers.

claims.claim: The asylum backlog is out of control.
claims.test: Supported if claims awaiting an initial decision at the latest quarter end are higher than a year earlier; partly if lower but still above 1.5 times the end-2019 level; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: 40,168 asylum claims were waiting for an initial decision on 30 June 2026, against 90,812 a year earlier, a peak of 175,457 on 30 June 2023 and 51,228 at the end of 2019. 11,014 had waited 12 months or more.

series.name: Asylum claims awaiting an initial decision (quarter ends)

notes: This is the backlog of first decisions only. Appeals waiting at the tribunal are held by the Ministry of Justice and are not in this data (backlog B-49).
The unit is claims as counted in the Home Office dataset (see DATA ISSUES IMM-DQ-01).

claims.claim: Almost everyone who claims asylum is granted it.
claims.test: Supported if the initial grant rate in the latest 12 months and the eventual grant rate for the 2022 claim cohort (after appeals) are both over 50%; partly if only one is; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: 38.1% of people who received an initial asylum decision in the year ending June 2026 were granted protection or other leave. Looking at everyone who claimed in 2022 and following their cases through appeal, 68.0% have now been granted (the initial grant rate for that group was 60.3%). The initial grant rate was 42% in 2025 and 76% in 2022.

series.name: Grant rate at initial decision, %

notes: The Home Office grant rate is grants divided by all initial decisions, including withdrawals and administrative outcomes.

claims.claim: Small boat arrivals are mostly people who are not genuine refugees.
claims.test: A factual question: grant rates at initial decision for small boat arrivals by nationality. 'Genuine refugee' is a legal finding made case by case, so the grant rate is shown, not a verdict.
claims.headline: For people who arrived by small boat, 47.7% of cases decided in the year ending June 2026 were granted (it was 55.7% the year before). The rate differs hugely by nationality, from 5% to 91% among the ten largest groups.

notes: Initial decisions, cases. The ten largest nationalities of small boat arrivals are shown. Rates move with the Home Office's country guidance (e.g. Syria after December 2024).

claims.claim: Many asylum claims are fraudulent.
claims.test: Cannot be tested: no published measure.
claims.headline: No official source measures fraud in asylum claims. A refused claim is not a fraudulent one (refusals include claims that fail the legal test in good faith), so the refusal rate cannot be read as a fraud rate. The Home Office does not publish counts of claims found to be deliberately false, and the NAO has not published one either. The nearest published facts are on age disputes (IMM-12), claims certified clearly unfounded (to 2024, table Asy_D08) and appeal outcomes (to 2023).
claims.why_not: No official source measures fraud in asylum claims. A refused claim is not a fraudulent one (refusals include claims that fail the legal test in good faith), so the refusal rate cannot be read as a fraud rate. The Home Office does not publish counts of claims found to be deliberately false, and the NAO has not published one either. The nearest published facts are on age disputes (IMM-12), claims certified clearly unfounded (to 2024, table Asy_D08) and appeal outcomes (to 2023).

claims.claim: Many people claiming to be children are really adults.
claims.test: Of initial Home Office age decisions on disputed-age cases that were closed in the latest four quarters, supported if more than 50% judged adult; partly if 30% to 50%; otherwise not supported. Covers only people whose age was disputed.
claims.headline: Between 2025 Q3 and 2026 Q2, the Home Office closed 5,914 initial decisions on disputed age: 3,073 (52.0%) were judged adult, 2,841 were treated as children. Of 2,406 later local authority assessments, 1,705 (70.9%) found the person to be a child.

notes: This covers only people whose age was disputed, not all asylum claimants. 'Treat as a child' means the person was given the benefit of the doubt, not that they were found to be a child.
Not every claimant who says they are under 18 is in this data.

claims.claim: Asylum seekers are the main driver of immigration.
claims.test: Supported if asylum claims in calendar 2025 are more than 50% of ONS gross immigration for the year to December 2025; partly if over 25%; otherwise not supported. Claims are not arrivals, so this is an indicator of scale.
claims.headline: 101,911 people claimed asylum in 2025, equal to 12.5% of the 813,000 people the ONS estimates immigrated in the year to December 2025 (provisional). The NAO puts the 2024 share at 11.4% and at 0.16% of the UK population. Net migration in the same year was 171,000.

notes: Claims are not arrivals: many claimants entered earlier on visas. The two series are close in time but not like-for-like.
The ONS figures are provisional.

claims.claim: Net migration is at record highs.
claims.test: Supported if the latest ONS net migration (rolling year) is at least as high as any earlier rolling year in the series from 2012; partly if within 25% of the peak; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: ONS provisional net migration is 171,000 for the year ending December 2025: 813,000 arrived and 642,000 left. The peak was 944,000 in the year ending March 2023, so net migration is now 82% below its peak.

series.name: Net long-term international migration, rolling years

notes: The latest figures are provisional and the ONS has revised recent years by more than 100,000 as travel data arrived: for the year ending December 2024 the first estimate was 431,000 and the completed estimate is 331,000 (ONS Table 5).
Includes people of all nationalities and all reasons (work, study, family, asylum, other).

claims.claim: The number of asylum seekers in hotels keeps going up.
claims.test: Supported if people in asylum hotels at the latest quarter end are more than 5% above a year earlier; partly if within 5% either way; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: 16,021 asylum seekers were in hotels on 30 June 2026, 17% of everyone supported (93,293). That is 50% fewer than a year earlier (32,041) and 71% below the peak of 56,018 on 30 September 2023.

series.name: Asylum seekers in hotels (quarter ends)

notes: 'Contingency accommodation - hotel' in the Home Office support data. Military and other large sites are counted under 'other contingency accommodation' (1,255 at the latest date).

claims.claim: Asylum hotels cost taxpayers millions of pounds every day.
claims.test: A factual question: audited or NAO-published hotel spending converted to a cost per day, with the NAO's per-person-per-night range. No threshold.
claims.headline: Hotels cost about £6.1 million a day in April to October 2024 (NAO: £1.3bn over 214 days), against £6.3 million a day in 2022-23 and £8.5 million forecast for 2023-24. At the NAO's 2023-24 price of £127 to £148 per person per night, today's 16,021 hotel residents would cost £0.74bn to £0.87bn a year (our illustration, not a published figure).

notes: Hotel costs after October 2024 are not published in an audited source we can use; the illustration multiplies today's occupancy by the NAO's 2023-24 price range.
Hotels are 76% of the contract cost but 35% of people (NAO, 2025).

claims.claim: The asylum system costs taxpayers billions of pounds a year.
claims.test: A factual question: the cost of asylum support from the Home Office's accounts and the NAO, set against total spending, the Home Office budget and debt interest. No threshold.
claims.headline: The Home Office's asylum support, resettlement and accommodation budget line cost £4.18bn in 2025-26 (budget £4.33bn), including £222m for Afghan resettlement. The NAO puts the direct cost of supporting people seeking asylum at £4.0bn in 2024-25. That is 0.31% of total government spending, 23% of the Home Office's resource budget, and 4% of what central government paid in debt interest. Spread over the roughly 107,244 people supported on average in 2024-25 it is about £37,298 per person per year (our calculation).

rows: Asylum support, resettlement and accommodation (Home Office resource spending)
Home Office annual report and accounts
Direct cost of supporting people seeking asylum
NAO, An analysis of the asylum system
Original 10-year estimate for the accommodation contracts
Current 10-year estimate for the accommodation contracts

notes: The Home Office line includes resettlement schemes (Afghan resettlement alone is £222m), so it is not only asylum.
The per-person figure divides a NAO cost by the mean of four quarter-end supported populations; it is an average, not a unit cost.

claims.claim: Private companies are making big profits out of asylum accommodation.
claims.test: Supported if the average supplier-reported profit margin is above the top of the Home Office's planned range (13%); partly if inside the range but at least one contract has exceeded its profit-share threshold; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: The NAO reports that the three accommodation suppliers' profit margin has averaged 7%, inside the Home Office's planned range of 5% to 13% and above the 3% to 7% operating profit in their published accounts. But 5 of the contracts have exceeded their profit-share thresholds, and the 10-year contract bill estimate has risen from £4.5bn to £15.3bn (3.4 times) as numbers supported grew.

bars.label: In suppliers' own accounts: high end

notes: Supplier-reported figures; the NAO did not audit them and the Home Office's own audit was still under way.
The NAO notes hotels may be more profitable than other accommodation, but the margin by accommodation type is not published.

claims.claim: Using barracks and military sites for asylum seekers saves money compared with hotels.
claims.test: Supported if the Home Office's own estimate (as reviewed by the NAO) of the large-site programme cost is lower than using hotels; not supported if it is higher.
claims.headline: The Home Office's own January 2024 analysis, reviewed by the NAO, was that its four large sites (Bibby Stockholm, Wethersfield, Scampton, Huddersfield) would cost about £46m more than hotels once sunk costs are counted, on a programme cost of £1,200m. Wethersfield's set-up cost rose from about £5m to £49m and Scampton's to £27m. The Northeye site at Bexhill was bought for £15.4m and was not operational when the NAO reported. At the latest count 1,255 people were in contingency accommodation other than hotels.

rows: Large sites programme, expected total cost
Expected cost beyond using hotels instead (incl. sunk costs)
Wethersfield set-up: original expectation then latest
Losses on sites developed but not used

notes: The NAO is reporting the Home Office's estimates, which it says contain significant uncertainty and depend on the hotel price assumed. Later events (the Bibby Stockholm closing in 2025, Home Office plans to use more large sites) are not in this assessment.

claims.claim: Some parts of the country take far more asylum seekers than others.
claims.test: Supported if the tenth of local authority areas with the most supported asylum seekers hold at least 25% of them and at least 10% of areas have none; partly if only one of the two holds; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: On 30 Jun 2026, 69,593 asylum seekers in Home Office dispersal or initial accommodation were placed in 318 of 361 local authority areas; 43 areas (12%) had none. The tenth of areas with the most hold 51% of all of them (an even spread would be 10%). The highest rate is Glasgow City with 5.8 per 1,000 residents; the national average is 1.0.
claims.unit: % in the top tenth of areas

notes: 1,058 supported people could not be matched to an area with a population figure (areas that changed code, or Northern Ireland/unknown).

Counts people in initial or dispersal accommodation (the definition behind the NAO figure of 70 areas with none in December 2024, which this method reproduces within one area). Bars are per 1,000 residents by English region.

claims.claim: Asylum seekers are being housed in the poorest areas.
claims.test: Supported if the most deprived third of English local authorities hold at least 1.5 times their population share of supported asylum seekers; partly if at least 1.15 times; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: The third of English local authorities that are most deprived (Index of Multiple Deprivation, average rank) hold 63% of asylum seekers in Home Office accommodation but 40% of the population, a ratio of 1.6. The least deprived third hold 8% of asylum seekers and 26% of residents.

bars.label: Most deprived third (people supported per 1,000 residents)
Least deprived third (people supported per 1,000 residents)

notes: Local authority level hides large differences inside areas; deprivation is the 2019 English index averaged over each authority.
England only. Asylum seekers may be placed in the cheapest housing, which tends to be in lower-income areas; this data cannot say why.

claims.claim: Resettlement schemes (Afghan, Syrian and others) are a major cost.
claims.test: A factual question: people resettled by scheme and the Home Office's Afghan resettlement cost. No threshold.
claims.headline: 73,532 people have been resettled through the UK's refugee resettlement schemes since 2010, 39,058 of them through the Afghan Resettlement Programme. The Home Office's Afghan resettlement costs were £222m in 2025-26 (£205m in 2024-25).

notes: Ukraine visa schemes and British National (Overseas) routes are separate tables and are not in this total.
Costs are the Home Office's only; other departments (local authorities, health, education) also bear costs.

claims.claim: Work visas are at record levels.
claims.test: Supported if work visas issued (entry clearance, including dependants) in 2025 are at least as many as in any year since 2015; partly if within 25% of the record; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: 260,430 work visas (all routes, including dependants) were issued in 2025, 58% below the record of 613,627 in 2023 and 1.4 times the 2019 level (192,559). Main applicants were 168,018 of the 2025 total.

series.name: Work visas issued per year (entry clearance, outside the UK)

notes: Entry clearance visas issued from outside the UK. Extensions and switches of visa inside the UK are separate Home Office tables (not loaded: backlog B-50). A visa issued is not an arrival.

claims.claim: Student visas are at record levels.
claims.test: Supported if study visas issued (entry clearance, including dependants) in 2025 are at least as many as in any year since 2015; partly if within 25% of the record; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: 427,340 study visas (all routes, including dependants) were issued in 2025, 31% below the record of 623,698 in 2022 and 1.1 times the 2019 level (404,410). Main applicants were 407,787 of the 2025 total.

series.name: Study visas issued per year (entry clearance, outside the UK)

notes: Entry clearance visas issued from outside the UK. Extensions and switches of visa inside the UK are separate Home Office tables (not loaded: backlog B-50). A visa issued is not an arrival.

claims.claim: Most health and care worker visas go to dependants, not workers.
claims.test: Supported if more than 50% of Health and Care Worker visas issued in 2025 went to dependants; partly if 30% to 50%; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: In 2025, 35,339 of 48,532 Health and Care Worker visas (73%) went to dependants of the worker and 13,193 to the workers themselves. For Skilled Worker visas, 40,656 of 73,066 (56%) were dependants. In 2023 care and health visas peaked at 348,157 (dependants 58%).

series.name: Health and Care Worker visas issued, main applicants

notes: Policy changed in 2024: most care workers can no longer bring dependants, so the 2025 and later pattern differs from 2023.

claims.claim: Foreign criminals are not being deported any more.
claims.test: Supported if foreign national offender returns in the latest 12 months are more than 10% below the 2015 to 2019 yearly average; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: 5,962 foreign national offenders were returned in the year ending June 2026 (5,333 the year before), against an average of 5,880 a year in 2015 to 2019 and a low of 2,706 in 2021.

series.name: Foreign national offender returns per calendar year

notes: The data count returns but not how many foreign national offenders are in the UK, so a rate of removal cannot be given.

claims.claim: Where are the asylum hotels?
claims.test: A factual question: asylum seekers in hotels by local authority area at the latest date, with the rate per 1,000 residents. No threshold.
claims.headline: On 30 Jun 2026, 16,021 people were in asylum hotels in 101 local authority areas. The twelve areas with most hold 42% of them; the largest is Hillingdon with 965.

notes: Local authority of the hotel, from the Home Office support data. Hotels used by the Home Office are not individually named in open data.

claims.claim: Which companies are paid for asylum accommodation?
claims.test: A factual question: asylum-related contract awards and payments over £25,000 to the accommodation and hotel-booking suppliers named in Home Office payment files. No threshold.
claims.headline: Home Office payment files list £478m to the named accommodation and hotel-booking suppliers (Clearsprings Ready Homes, Serco, Mears, Corporate Travel Management North), and contract notices for asylum work include GTD Healthcare (£675m ceiling for Enhanced Primary Care Services for Asylum Seekers).

claims.claim: The top 1% of earners pay a quarter of all income tax.
claims.test: Supported if the top 1% of Income Tax payers paid at least 25% of all Income Tax in the latest survey year (2023-24); partly if at least 15%; otherwise not supported. Groups are percentiles of people liable to Income Tax, ranked by total income.
claims.headline: The top 1% of Income Tax payers (367,000 people with total income above about £207,000) paid 27.2% of all Income Tax in 2023-24 (£75bn of £274bn) while receiving 12.4% of taxable income. Their share was 21.3% in 1999-00.

series.name: Share of all Income Tax paid by the top 1% of taxpayers, %

notes: Percentile groups are of people liable to Income Tax (about 36.7 million), not of all adults. Total income includes pay, pensions, interest, dividends and self-employment profit before tax.
Years from 2024-25 are HMRC projections.

claims.claim: The top 10% pay most of the income tax.
claims.test: Supported if the top 10% of Income Tax payers paid more than 50% of all Income Tax in 2023-24; partly if at least 35%; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: The top 10% of Income Tax payers (3,670,000 people with total income above about £67,400) paid 59.1% of all Income Tax in 2023-24 while receiving 34.0% of taxable income. Their share was 50.3% in 1999-00.

series.name: Share of all Income Tax paid by the top 10% of taxpayers, %

notes: Percentile groups are of people liable to Income Tax, not of all adults.

claims.claim: Half of taxpayers pay almost no income tax.
claims.test: Supported if the bottom half of Income Tax payers paid less than 10% of all Income Tax in 2023-24; partly if less than 20%; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: The bottom half of Income Tax payers (18,350,000 people with total income below about £29,700) paid 9.9% of all Income Tax in 2023-24 (£27bn) while receiving 24.9% of taxable income. Their share was 11.6% in 1999-00.

series.name: Share of all Income Tax paid by the bottom half of taxpayers, %

notes: They still pay National Insurance, VAT and other taxes, which this table does not include (see the all-taxes claim by income group). Adults with income below the personal allowance are not Income Tax payers and are not in the 36.7 million.

claims.claim: What do you need to earn to be in the top 10%, 5% or 1%, and how many people is that?
claims.test: A factual question: the income at each percentile boundary among Income Tax payers, the number of people in each group, their share of taxable income and of Income Tax, and the average Income Tax each pays. No threshold.
claims.headline: In 2023-24 the 36.7 million people liable to Income Tax had a median total income of £29,700 and a mean of £41,700. To be in the top 10% a taxpayer needed about £67,400; for the top 1%, £207,000.

columns: Total income at the group's boundary

notes: Total income is before tax and includes all taxable income, not only salary. Boundaries are the percentile points from HMRC Table 3.1a / 2.4. People counts are the group's share of all Income Tax payers.

claims.claim: High earners pay a lower rate of tax than ordinary workers.
claims.test: Supported if the average Income Tax rate (tax divided by total income) for people with total income of £500,000 or more is lower than for people with £50,000 to £100,000, in 2023-24. Income Tax only; the all-taxes comparison is a separate claim.
claims.headline: People with total income above £500,000 paid 39.9% of their income in Income Tax in 2023-24; those with £50,000 to £99,999 paid 18.9%. The average across all 36.7 million taxpayers was 17.9%.

notes: Income Tax only. National Insurance falls to 2% above the upper earnings limit, VAT is paid on spending, and capital gains, wealth and avoidance are outside this table. See the all-taxes claim for the combined picture by income group.
Bars are the average Income Tax as a percentage of total income, by range of total income (lower limit), for the latest survey year.

claims.claim: More and more people are being dragged into the higher rate of tax.
claims.test: Supported if the number of higher-rate Income Tax payers in 2023-24 is more than 50% above 2010-11; partly if more than 20% above; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: 5.8 million people paid Income Tax at the higher rate in 2023-24, up from 3.0 million in 2010-11 (+91%), while all taxpayers rose +17%. Higher-rate payers were 15.7% of taxpayers, against 9.6% then; HMRC projects 7.3 million in 2025-26. Additional-rate payers rose from 0.24 million to 0.89 million.

series.name: Higher-rate Income Tax payers, millions (UK)

notes: Thresholds have been frozen in cash terms, so pay rises move more people into higher bands (fiscal drag); this data shows the count, not the cause. The Scottish rates differ from the rest of the UK.
The count is of people liable to Income Tax in the survey year; 2024-25 onwards are HMRC projections.

claims.claim: Who are the Income Tax payers: how many are women, how many are over 65?
claims.test: A factual question: counts of Income Tax payers by sex and age from HMRC Table 2.1. No threshold.
claims.headline: Of 36.7 million Income Tax payers in 2023-24, 19.9 million (54.4%) were men and 16.7 million (45.6%) women; 8.6 million (23.4%) were aged 65 or over. The number of taxpayers aged 65+ was 4.9 million in 2010-11.

bars.label: At or above state pension age

notes: Counts of people, not the amount of tax each group pays: HMRC's published tables give amounts by income range and percentile, not by sex or age.

claims.claim: London and the South East pay most of the tax.
claims.test: Supported if London and the South East have at least 1.5 times their population share of higher-rate Income Tax payers; partly if at least 1.2 times; otherwise not supported. Counts of taxpayers, not amounts.
claims.headline: London and the South East have 27% of the UK population but 37% of higher-rate taxpayers (ratio 1.4). Higher-rate payers are 23% of London's taxpayers and 11% of the North East's.

notes: Counts by place of residence of the taxpayer from HMRC Table 2.2. The amount of tax by region is not published in these tables.
Population is the ONS mid-year estimate for the latest year loaded.

claims.claim: The poor pay a bigger share of their income in tax than the rich.
claims.test: Supported if the poorest fifth of households paid more than 2 percentage points more of their gross income in all taxes (Income Tax, National Insurance, Council Tax, VAT, duties) than the richest fifth in 2023/24; partly if within 2 points either way; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: Households in the poorest fifth paid 36.7% of their gross income in all taxes in 2023/24 (direct 15.7%, indirect such as VAT 21.0%); the richest fifth paid 36.2% (direct 28.8%, indirect 7.5%). The lowest burden is in the 3rd fifth at 30.2%.
claims.unit: % of gross income paid in all taxes (poorest fifth)

bars.label: Poorest fifth (gross £23,495 a year per household)
Richest fifth (gross £143,345 a year per household)

notes: Households ranked by equivalised disposable income (ONS ETB Table 2a). Taxes include Income Tax, employee and employer National Insurance (the latter as an indirect tax), Council Tax, VAT, duties and business rates passed on to prices; the ETB attributes taxes to households by assumption.
A household's tax is shown as a share of gross income (original income plus cash benefits).

claims.claim: Over half the country takes more out of the system than it pays in.
claims.test: Supported if more than 50% of people in 2023/24 lived in households that received more in benefits (cash plus services like the NHS and schools, at cost) than they paid in taxes; partly if more than 40%; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: In 2023/24, 53.3% of people (35.8 million) lived in households that received more in benefits (cash and services such as the NHS and schools) than they paid in taxes: 45.8% of non-retired people and 90.1% of retired people. Counting cash benefits only, 2 of the 10 income groups receive more than they pay. Counting cash and services, 6 groups are net recipients: the bottom, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th groups.

claims.claim: Working households pay for pensioners.
claims.test: Supported if non-retired households in aggregate paid more in taxes than they received in benefits and services, and retired households received more than they paid, in 2023/24 (survey estimates).
claims.headline: In 2023/24 the average non-retired household paid £25,652 in taxes and received £21,955 (cash £6,097 plus services £15,858), a net contribution of £3,697; across 21.2 million households that is about £79bn. The average retired household paid £10,363 and received £29,240 (State Pension and other cash £16,617), a net receipt of £18,877; across 7.2 million households about £136bn.
claims.unit: £ billion net contribution of non-retired households

notes: Survey estimates: average per household times households, not an accounting total. ETB aggregates differ from administrative totals (see the check against HMRC receipts in DATA ISSUES TAX-DQ-02). Taxes here exclude corporation tax and other taxes not attributed to households.
Non-retired households include children, students, disabled people and unemployed adults as well as workers.

claims.section: Spending, borrowing and the tax base
claims.claim: Most of the welfare bill goes to pensioners, not the unemployed.
claims.test: Supported if pensioners received more than 50% of DWP benefit expenditure in the latest outturn year (2024-25); partly if more than 35%; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: Of £289bn spent on benefits in 2024-25, £165bn (57%) went to pensioners (State Pension alone £137bn), £120bn (41%) to working-age people and £4.6bn (2%) to children. Universal Credit cost £66.7bn; Jobseeker's Allowance, the main unemployment benefit, £0.31bn.
claims.unit: % of benefit spending going to pensioners

notes: DWP benefit expenditure only (Great Britain basis mostly); the NHS, schools and social care are not benefits and are not in this figure. Working-age benefits include disability and housing support for people in work and out of work.
Benefits for working-age people include Universal Credit paid to people in work, so this is not a count of unemployed people.

claims.claim: Ordinary households, not businesses, pay most of the tax.
claims.test: Supported if taxes on individuals' income and gains plus taxes on their spending (VAT and duties) are more than 60% of HMRC receipts in 2025-26; partly if more than 45%. Employer National Insurance and company profit taxes are shown separately, grouped by who the law makes liable.
claims.headline: Of £938bn collected by HMRC in 2025-26, £412bn (44%) was tax on individuals' income and gains (Income Tax £327bn, of which PAYE £278bn), £247bn (26%) was VAT and duties paid when people spend, £148bn (16%) was employers' National Insurance and the Apprenticeship Levy, and £101bn (11%) was tax on company profits (Corporation Tax £95bn).
claims.unit: % of HMRC receipts paid by households

bars.label: Individuals: Income Tax, employee NICs, capital gains, inheritance
Consumers: VAT, fuel, alcohol, tobacco, other duties
Employers: employer National Insurance, Apprenticeship Levy
Companies' profits: Corporation Tax and sector levies
Everything else: stamp duties, environmental taxes, penalties, other

notes: Grouped by who the law makes liable to pay. Who really bears a tax (for example employer National Insurance falling on wages, or VAT on customers) is a matter of economic research, not of the receipts data.
HMRC receipts exclude Council Tax and business rates, which are paid to local government.

Groups: individuals = Income Tax, PAYE NIC1 (EMP'ee), SA NIC2&4, Capital Gains Tax, Inheritance Tax; consumers = Value Added Tax, Hydrocarbon Oil (Fuel duties), Tobacco Duties, Beer Duties, Wines Duties, Spirits Duties, Cider Duties, Betting & Gaming, Insurance Premium Tax, Air Passenger Duty, Customs Duties.

claims.claim: Companies pay more corporation tax than ever.
claims.test: Supported if onshore corporation tax as a share of GDP in 2025-26 is at least as high as in any earlier year in the OBR series; partly if within 0.3 percentage points of the highest; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: Onshore corporation tax raised £97.8bn in 2025-26, 3.19% of GDP. The highest share since 1999-00 was 3.21% in 2023-24; the lowest was 1.89%. The OBR forecasts 3.43% by 2030-31.

series.name: Onshore corporation tax, % of GDP

notes: Onshore corporation tax includes the bank surcharge; North Sea (offshore) taxes are separate. Receipts depend on rates, profits and allowances (for example full expensing).

claims.claim: Billions of tax go uncollected.
claims.test: A factual question: HMRC's estimate of the tax gap and who it is attributed to. No threshold.
claims.headline: HMRC estimates the tax gap (tax owed but not paid) at £59.2bn in 2024-25, 6.4% of the £924bn it should have collected. Small businesses account for £36.7bn (62%), large businesses £7.1bn and the wealthy £3.6bn. By tax: Corporation Tax £21.0bn, Income Tax, NICs and CGT £20.9bn, VAT £12.1bn.

notes: The tax gap is an estimate by HMRC with a margin of error, including evasion, avoidance, error and the hidden economy. It is not the amount that could realistically be recovered.

claims.section: Spending, borrowing and the tax base
claims.claim: Where does each pound of tax go?
claims.test: A factual question: receipts against total managed expenditure and borrowing, and spending by function. No threshold.
claims.headline: In 2025-26 government spent £1,366bn and raised £1,231bn in receipts, so receipts covered 90p of every £1 spent and 10p was borrowed (£134bn). Debt interest took 9p of every £1 of receipts. Of spending on services, social protection (mainly pensions and benefits) was 33%, then health 21% and general public services 13%.

claims.section: Spending, borrowing and the tax base
claims.claim: Tax can no longer pay for public services without borrowing.
claims.test: Supported if receipts are below spending excluding debt interest in 2025-26 and the OBR forecast has no year of surplus before interest; partly if there is a deficit now but the OBR forecasts a surplus before interest within its horizon; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: Excluding debt interest, government spent £25bn more than it raised in 2025-26 (0.8% of GDP); the full borrowing figure of £134bn includes £109bn of interest. The OBR's March 2026 forecast has receipts exceeding non-interest spending from 2027-28, reaching a surplus of £78bn in 2030-31.
claims.unit: £ billion primary balance (receipts minus spending excluding debt interest)

series.name: Receipts minus spending excluding debt interest, £ billion

notes: A forecast, not data: the OBR's projection assumes announced policies and its economic forecast. Primary balance uses central government debt interest net of the Asset Purchase Facility as the OBR defines it.

claims.section: Spending, borrowing and the tax base
claims.claim: There are too few workers to support the number of people not working.
claims.test: A factual question: population by age group, projected Income Tax payers and benefit spending. A count of people not working needs labour market data (backlog B-53), so no verdict is given.
claims.headline: In mid-2025 the UK had 43.7 million people aged 16 to 64, 13.5 million aged 65 or over and 12.3 million under 16: 3.2 working-age people for each person aged 65+. HMRC projects 39.8 million Income Tax payers in 2025-26 (9.6 million of them aged 65+), paying £329bn: about £8,266 each. DWP benefit spending was £289bn in 2024-25.
claims.unit: people aged 16 to 64 for each person aged 65 or over

notes: Not everyone aged 16 to 64 works: students, carers, sick and disabled people and the unemployed are in that group. Labour market data (employment, inactivity by reason) is backlog item B-53, so a count of people not working is not given here.
Only mid-2025 population by age is loaded, so no trend is shown (a long series is backlog item B-53).

claims.claim: Immigrants and foreign nationals pay less tax than they take out.
claims.test: Cannot be tested with open data: no published measure of tax or benefits by nationality.
claims.headline: HMRC and DWP do not publish tax paid or benefits received by nationality or country of birth. The ETB shows households by income, age, retirement, tenure and region but not nationality. Home Office and ONS data count visas and migrants, not their tax. Only research using linked administrative data (for example the OBR's migration scenarios or the Migration Advisory Committee's fiscal impact work) addresses it, and those estimates depend on assumptions.
claims.why_not: HMRC and DWP do not publish tax paid or benefits received by nationality or country of birth. The ETB shows households by income, age, retirement, tenure and region but not nationality. Home Office and ONS data count visas and migrants, not their tax. Only research using linked administrative data (for example the OBR's migration scenarios or the Migration Advisory Committee's fiscal impact work) addresses it, and those estimates depend on assumptions.

claims.claim: The squeezed middle is being taxed hardest.
claims.test: Cannot be tested with the published tables alone.
claims.headline: 'Squeezed middle' mixes tax with housing costs, childcare and the loss of benefits as income rises (marginal rates). The open tables give average tax rates by income (TAX-06, TAX-10), not the marginal rate on the next pound earned or the effect of losing Child Benefit and tax-free childcare; computing those needs a tax-and-benefit model such as the Institute for Fiscal Studies' TAXBEN or HMRC's, which is not open data. The ETB median income series by stage of the tax system (Table 20) is a route to part of it.
claims.why_not: 'Squeezed middle' mixes tax with housing costs, childcare and the loss of benefits as income rises (marginal rates). The open tables give average tax rates by income (TAX-06, TAX-10), not the marginal rate on the next pound earned or the effect of losing Child Benefit and tax-free childcare; computing those needs a tax-and-benefit model such as the Institute for Fiscal Studies' TAXBEN or HMRC's, which is not open data. The ETB median income series by stage of the tax system (Table 20) is a route to part of it.

claims.claim: Councils in deprived areas spend much more per head.
claims.test: Among all-purpose councils (London boroughs, metropolitan districts, unitary authorities), supported if the most deprived third spend at least 1.25 times as much per head (excluding schools, police and fire) as the least deprived third; partly if at least 1.1 times.
claims.headline: Among 132 all-purpose councils (London boroughs, metropolitan districts and unitary authorities), the most deprived third spend £1,315 per head on services other than schools, police and fire, against £1,260 for the least deprived third: 1.04 times as much. Including education the figures are £2,183 and £2,395.
claims.unit: x (most deprived third / least deprived third)

notes: Net current expenditure per head from each council's latest submitted return (2023-24 to 2025-26) divided by mid-2025 population. Deprivation is the English Indices of Deprivation average score for the authority.
Deprivation, age, social care need and the cost of providing services all differ between areas; this compares spending, not need or value.

claims.claim: Adult social care costs are driven by an ageing population.
claims.test: Across all-purpose councils, supported if the correlation between adult social care spending per head and the share of residents aged 65 or over is at least 0.5; partly if at least 0.25.
claims.headline: Across 132 all-purpose councils, adult social care spending per head has a correlation of 0.30 with the share of residents aged 65 or over (and 0.13 with deprivation). Spending per head averages £477; it ranges from £323 to £884.

notes: Correlation across authorities (1 = move together, 0 = unrelated); the table lists the six councils spending most per head. Census 2021 age shares against 2023-24 to 2025-26 spending.
Councils differ in how much social care they commission, what they charge and what NHS funds, so this does not measure need.

claims.claim: Children's social care is the fastest-growing council cost.
claims.test: Like for like across English councils that submitted both 2017-18 and 2024-25, supported if children's social care had the highest real-terms growth of the major services; partly if it ranked in the top three; otherwise not supported.
claims.headline: Like for like across 306 English councils that submitted both years, spending on children's social care grew +83% in real terms between 2017-18 and 2024-25 (£8.3bn to £15.2bn in 2025-26 prices), ranking 2 of 10 major services. Adult social care +70%; all services +52%. The fastest-growing major service is housing (excluding benefits) (+117%).

notes: Net current expenditure, prices converted to 2025-26 with the Treasury's GDP deflator. Only authorities that submitted a return in both years are included so that growth is not caused by missing returns.
Some services were reclassified, passed between tiers or funded by new grants over this period; growth in spending is not growth in demand or quality.

claims.claim: Councils rely more and more on Council Tax.
claims.test: Supported if Council Tax funded at least 2 percentage points more of English councils' net revenue expenditure in 2024-25 than in 2017-18 (like-for-like authorities); partly if any increase.
claims.headline: Council Tax funded 62.2% of English councils' net revenue expenditure in 2024-25, up from 59.8% in 2017-18 (like-for-like authorities): +2.3 percentage points. Retained business rates financed 31.6%.
claims.unit: % of net revenue expenditure funded by Council Tax

series.name: Council Tax requirement as % of net revenue expenditure

notes: Net revenue expenditure after specific grants; the remainder is retained business rates, Revenue Support Grant and other grants. Authorities that submitted in the first year are tracked to the last year.

claims.claim: Council Tax bills vary enormously from place to place.
claims.test: A factual question: the range of average Band D Council Tax between English all-purpose authorities for 2026-27. No threshold.
claims.headline: Average Band D Council Tax for 2026-27 (including adult social care) ranges from £518 in Wandsworth to £2,396 in Gateshead across 132 all-purpose authorities; the median is £2,016. The gap between the highest and lowest is 4.6 times.

notes: Average Band D including parish precepts and the adult social care precept, from MHCLG Council Tax levels set 2026-27 (tables 8a to 8c). Bills differ because house values, the tax base and funding differ, not only because of how well councils are run.
Districts in two-tier areas set a district Band D; the county precept is added on top, so district-only figures are not directly comparable.

claims.claim: Government money is concentrated in London.
claims.test: Supported if London's share of placed supplier payments in 2025-26 (excluding funding to other public bodies and accounting entries) is at least 1.5 times its share of the UK population; partly if at least 1.15 times.
claims.headline: Of £42bn of 2025-26 payments to suppliers and other recipients that could be placed by postcode (excluding money passed to other public bodies and accounting entries), 30% went to recipients in London, which has 13% of the UK population: 2.3 times its share. London's share of grants was 21% (of £6bn placed).

notes: Money is placed where the recipient's postcode is (the postcode in the payment file, otherwise the supplier's Companies House registered office). A contractor's head office is not where the work or the benefit happens, so payments to large firms land in London and a few other places.

Only about half of payment value can be placed (see the coverage table in place_payment_coverage). Payments to NHS England, councils and other public bodies are excluded here; they are in the table with their own kind.

claims.claim: Poorer constituencies get less government money than richer ones.
claims.test: In England, comparing the median constituency per resident in the most deprived third with the least deprived third, supported if supplier payments placed by recipient postcode are no more than 0.8 times as much in the most deprived third; partly if no more than 1.0 times.
claims.headline: In England, the median constituency in the most deprived third received £35 per resident of 2025-26 payments to suppliers and other recipients placed by recipient postcode, against £131 in the least deprived third: 0.27 times as much. Medians are used because a few constituencies hold the head offices of very large recipients.
claims.unit: x (most deprived third / least deprived third, median)

bars.label: Most deprived third of constituencies (median £ per resident)
Middle third of constituencies (median £ per resident)
Least deprived third of constituencies (median £ per resident)

notes: Constituency deprivation is the local authority Indices of Deprivation average score weighted by residents (an estimate). Per-head amounts divide by Census 2021 residents.
Where the recipient is registered is not where the money is spent; this is a distribution of recipient addresses, not of local benefit.

claims.claim: Grants go to the poorest areas.
claims.test: In England, supported if the median constituency in the most deprived third receives at least 1.25 times the grant money per resident of the least deprived third (grants placed by recipient postcode); partly if at least 1.0 times.
claims.headline: Grants in the Government Grants Register placed by recipient postcode amount to a median £1,270 per resident in the most deprived third of English constituencies, against £1,107 in the least deprived third: 1.15 times as much.
claims.unit: x (most deprived third / least deprived third, median)

bars.label: Most deprived third of constituencies (median £ per resident)
Middle third of constituencies (median £ per resident)
Least deprived third of constituencies (median £ per resident)

notes: Grants awarded in the years loaded (see grant_stats). Grants to councils and large charities register at their headquarters.
Deprivation is an estimate for constituencies, built from local authority averages.

claims.claim: Which constituencies receive the most government money?
claims.test: A factual question: constituencies ranked by 2025-26 supplier payments placed by recipient postcode, with the largest recipient in each. No threshold.
claims.headline: The constituencies where the most 2025-26 supplier payments land (by recipient postcode) are Cities of London and Westminster, Reading West and Mid Berkshire, Holborn and St Pancras. Cities of London and Westminster received £7,523m, largely because of who is registered there.

rows: Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West

notes: Excludes payments passed to other public bodies and accounting entries. Recipients are placed at the postcode in the payment file, else their registered office.

claims.claim: Some constituencies have far more pensioners than others.
claims.test: A factual question: the share of residents aged 65 and over by constituency, highest and lowest eight. No threshold.
claims.headline: The share of residents aged 65 or over ranges across 575 constituencies from 5.0% (Poplar and Limehouse) to 34.6% (Christchurch); England 18.4%, Wales 21.3%. Retired people are 21.5% of England's adults aged 16 and over.

notes: Census 2021 (usual residents, March 2021), added up from output areas to the 2024 constituency boundaries (best fit).

claims.claim: Long-term sickness and disability are concentrated in a few constituencies.
claims.test: A factual question: the share of adults economically inactive because of long-term sickness or disability, highest and lowest eight constituencies. No threshold.
claims.headline: The share of adults economically inactive because of long-term sickness or disability ranges across 575 constituencies from 1.6% (Harpenden and Berkhamsted) to 9.7% (Blaenau Gwent and Rhymney); England 4.1%, Wales 5.9%.

notes: Census 2021 economic activity (week before 21 March 2021). The census counts people, not benefit claims, so this is related to but not the same as PIP, ESA or UC health claims.

claims.claim: Disability rates differ hugely between constituencies.
claims.test: A factual question: the share of residents disabled under the Equality Act by constituency, highest and lowest eight. No threshold.
claims.headline: The share of residents disabled under the Equality Act ranges across 575 constituencies from 10.6% (Battersea) to 25.8% (Clacton); England 17.3%, Wales 21.6%.

notes: Self-reported long-term health problem or disability that limits day-to-day activities (Census 2021). Not a count of benefit claimants.

claims.claim: Some constituencies have very high shares of people born abroad.
claims.test: A factual question: the share of residents born outside the UK by constituency, highest and lowest eight. No threshold.
claims.headline: The share of residents born outside the UK ranges across 575 constituencies from 2.6% (Staffordshire Moorlands) to 62.2% (Brent West); England 17.4%, Wales 6.9%.

notes: Census 2021 country of birth. 'Born abroad' includes people who have lived here for decades and British citizens; recent arrivals are measured separately (arrived under 5 years).

claims.claim: Where are the most recent arrivals living?
claims.test: A factual question: the share of residents who had arrived in the UK less than five years before the 2021 census, highest and lowest eight constituencies. No threshold.
claims.headline: The share of residents who arrived in the UK in the five years before the census ranges across 575 constituencies from 0.4% (Staffordshire Moorlands) to 22.6% (Cities of London and Westminster); England 4.2%, Wales 1.7%.

notes: Length of residence under five years at March 2021: it includes students and workers as well as other migrants and cannot separate asylum seekers or visa types. The census predates the 2022-24 surge in arrivals.

claims.claim: Religion varies sharply between constituencies: where are the Muslim communities?
claims.test: A factual question: the share of residents who are Muslim by constituency, highest and lowest eight. No threshold.
claims.headline: The share of residents who say their religion is Islam ranges across 575 constituencies from 0.1% (St Austell and Newquay) to 58.7% (Bradford West); England 6.7%, Wales 2.2%.

notes: Census 2021 religion question was voluntary; 6% of people did not answer in England and Wales.

claims.claim: Where are the least religious constituencies?
claims.test: A factual question: the share of residents with no religion by constituency, highest and lowest eight. No threshold.
claims.headline: The share of residents reporting no religion ranges across 575 constituencies from 7.1% (East Ham) to 61.3% (Rhondda and Ogmore); England 36.7%, Wales 46.5%.

notes: Census 2021 religion question was voluntary.

claims.claim: Where is unemployment highest?
claims.test: A factual question: the census unemployment rate by constituency, highest and lowest eight. No threshold.
claims.headline: The census unemployment rate (unemployed as a share of the economically active) ranges across 575 constituencies from 2.9% (Skipton and Ripon) to 16.3% (Birmingham Ladywood); England 5.7%, Wales 5.5%.

rows: Birmingham Hodge Hill and Solihull North

notes: Census 2021 was taken in March 2021 during Covid restrictions and furlough, so employment and unemployment differ from the Labour Force Survey and from today.

claims.claim: Universal Credit claims are concentrated in a few places.
claims.test: Supported if the tenth of local authorities in England and Wales with the highest rate of people on Universal Credit (per person aged 15 to 64) hold at least 2 times their share of the working-age population in UC claimants; partly if at least 1.5 times.
claims.headline: The 32 local authorities in England and Wales with the highest Universal Credit rate hold 21% of the 7.7 million people on UC in these areas but 14% of the population aged 15 to 64 (1.5 times their share). The highest rate is Blackpool at 34 people on UC per 100 aged 15 to 64; the lowest is City of London at 8.

notes: DWP's own count of people on Universal Credit (all ages 16 and over, including people in work), divided by the 2021 census population aged 15 to 64, so the rate is approximate and can exceed the working-age share in places where the population has grown.

claims.claim: Asylum seekers are housed where most residents were born abroad.
claims.test: Across local authorities, supported if the correlation between asylum seekers in Home Office accommodation per 1,000 residents and the share of residents born abroad is at least 0.5; partly if at least 0.25.
claims.headline: Across 318 local authorities in England and Wales, the number of asylum seekers in Home Office accommodation per 1,000 residents has a correlation of -0.04 with the share of residents born abroad, and 0.64 with deprivation (England). A positive value means more asylum seekers are housed where more residents were born abroad.

notes: Local authority level: constituencies are not used because the asylum support data are published by authority. Born abroad is from the 2021 census, asylum accommodation is at the date shown.
Correlation across authorities shows association, not cause: dispersal policy places people where housing is cheap and available.

claims.claim: How many Personal Independence Payment (PIP) claimants are there in each constituency?
claims.test: A factual question: PIP cases with entitlement per 100 residents aged 15 to 64, by constituency, highest and lowest eight, with the Great Britain total. No threshold.

claims.claim: Constituency and local authority figures can be rolled up and compared.

claims.section: What the state pays in benefits
claims.claim: How much does the state pay out in benefits, and where does it go?
claims.test: A factual question: our annualised estimate of spending on nine DWP benefits for Great Britain, by benefit and by nation, compared with DWP's own expenditure tables. No threshold.
claims.headline: Across nine DWP benefits, the yearly rate of spending at each benefit's latest date is about £309bn for Great Britain and State Pension paid abroad: State Pension £146bn, Universal Credit £88bn, Personal Independence Payment £30bn, Housing Benefit £12bn. Nations: England £265bn, Scotland £21bn, Wales £17bn. This includes £5.7bn of State Pension paid to people living abroad. DWP's own expenditure tables put the same nine at £301bn for 2025-26 (a forecast); ours is +3% because caseloads and awards are higher at the later dates.
claims.as_at: latest period of each benefit (March to July 2026)

notes: Annualised = cases at the date × average award × 52 (Universal Credit: households × monthly payment × 12). It is a yearly rate, not cash paid in a financial year; DWP's tables are cash for 2025-26. Child Benefit, tax credits, Winter Fuel Payment and others are not included.
A person can receive several of these benefits, so cases are not people.
Employment and Support Allowance is below DWP's total because this count covers the cases in DWP's 2021-geography tables only (see data issue DWP-SX-02).

claims.claim: Why do Universal Credit payments differ so much between households?
claims.test: A factual question: average monthly Universal Credit payment per household by family type and by the elements the household is entitled to (children, housing, limited capability for work, carer, disabled child), Great Britain. No threshold.
claims.headline: 7.15 million households received Universal Credit in May 2026, at an average of £1,020 a month. The amount is built from elements: a single adult without children averaged £757, a single parent £1,341. Households entitled to extra elements (children, housing costs, limited capability for work because of illness or disability, caring) average more because the elements add to the payment; earnings then reduce it.

notes: Household payment amounts are after earnings have reduced them and after any deductions; households with the same elements can receive different amounts. The average is not what a typical household receives.
The categories overlap (a household can have a child element, a housing element and a limited capability for work element together), so groups do not add up to the total.

claims.claim: What are Personal Independence Payments paid for?
claims.test: A factual question: PIP cases and average weekly award by main disabling condition, and by daily living and mobility award level, Great Britain. No threshold.

claims.claim: How many people does the state employ, and how small a part of that are civil servants?
claims.test: A factual question: UK public sector employment (ONS headcount) by industry and sector for the latest quarter, with the Civil Service share. No threshold.
claims.headline: 6.21 million people worked in the UK public sector in June 2026 (ONS, headcount). The Civil Service was 557,000 of them (9.0%): the NHS (2,068,000, 33%) and education (1,664,000) are 3.7 and 3.0 times its size. Total public sector employment was +668 thousand and the Civil Service +109 thousand compared with June 2019.

rows: Public corporations (such as the BBC and Network Rail)

Support staff, FTE

claims.claim: There are fewer police officers than there used to be.
claims.test: A factual question: police officers (FTE) in England and Wales at each March since 2003, the peak and low, officers per 100,000 residents by force. No threshold.
claims.headline: England and Wales had 145,886 full-time-equivalent police officers at March 2026 (234,441 including police staff, PCSOs and designated officers), 236 officers per 100,000 residents. Officer numbers were 143,769 in March 2009, fell 15% to 122,405 in March 2018, recovered to 147,745 in March 2024 and are -1% against that peak. By force, Metropolitan Police has the most officers per 100,000 residents (347) and Lincolnshire the fewest (152).

Excludes the British Transport Police, National Crime Agency and officers on central service from the force table; Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own forces.

claims.claim: The armed forces have been cut to the bone.
claims.test: A factual question: UK Regular Forces strength quarterly since April 2012, the reserves and Gurkhas, and MoD civil servants alongside service personnel. No threshold.
claims.headline: The UK Regular Forces had 137,482 personnel on 1 July 2026 (-24% since April 2012); with Gurkhas and the reserves the armed forces had 182,984. In April 2026 the MoD employed 55,351 civil servants (FTE) alongside 148,779 service personnel: 204,130 in all. Officers were 20% of the regular forces.

Armed forces personnel are not on the Civil Service payroll; this is one of the groups the ONS counts as 'HM Forces' in public sector employment.

claims.section: What the state pays in benefits
claims.claim: Universal Credit has ballooned.
claims.test: A factual question: people on Universal Credit each month since June 2016 (DWP Stat-Xplore), the groups they are in, and PIP cases with entitlement since April 2020. No threshold.
claims.headline: 8,359,744 people were on Universal Credit in May 2026, up from 513,544 in May 2017 (16.3 times as many) and 5,938,916 in May 2021. 51% have no work requirements and 19% are searching for work; in April 2026, 38% had earnings from employment or self-employment. PIP cases with entitlement went from 2,242,320 in Aug-19 to 4,092,185 in Jul-26.

series.name: People on Universal Credit (monthly)

notes: Universal Credit has been rolled out in stages since 2013 and replaced six older benefits, so growth mixes new claims, people moved from the old benefits (the 'managed migration') and the pandemic. The count is of people, not households (the payment is per household).

The 'employment' share is DWP's indicator of earnings from PAYE or self-employment in the month; it is filled with a lag (the latest month is not available). 'No work requirements' is a rule-based group (health, caring, young children) and includes people who also work (DWP-SX-03).

claims.section: What the state pays in benefits
claims.claim: Hundreds of thousands of people start claiming Universal Credit every month.
claims.test: A factual question: starts on Universal Credit per month and in the last 12 months compared with the 12 before, by age and gender, against the number on Universal Credit. No threshold.
claims.headline: There were 2,225,323 starts on Universal Credit in the 12 months to May 2026 (185,444 a month on average), against 2,512,930 in the 12 months before (-11%). Over the same period the number of people on Universal Credit was 8,359,744: more people start each year than are on it, because many claims are short or people leave and re-claim.

series.name: Starts on Universal Credit per month

notes: A start is DWP's count of a person beginning a Universal Credit claim; one person can start more than once in a year, so starts are not new individuals. UC starts are published nationally and by Jobcentre Plus office only, not by constituency or authority (DWP-SX-03).
Most starts are not 'new to benefits': people also move onto Universal Credit from older benefits or after a gap in work.

claims.section: What the state pays in benefits
claims.claim: Benefit claimants are being sanctioned in large numbers.
claims.test: A factual question: Universal Credit claimants with a sanction applied in the latest month, as a share of all claimants and of those with work requirements, by work requirement group, and the monthly series. No threshold.
claims.headline: In May 2026, 106,589 Universal Credit claimants had a sanction applied: 1.3% of all 8,359,744 claimants, but 3.5% of the 2,903,899 who have work requirements (and 6.1% of those in the 'searching for work' group, which accounts for 89% of sanctions). The monthly count was lowest at 4,171 in February 2021 and highest at 137,435 in September 2023.

claims.section: How council spending fits the national total
claims.claim: Council spending is on top of the £1.36 trillion national total.
claims.test: A factual question: the Treasury's Total Managed Expenditure for 2025-26 (PESA table 1.11) with its local government department and its locally financed expenditure line, set against English councils' net current expenditure from their own returns. No threshold.
claims.headline: No: the £1.36tn of Total Managed Expenditure in 2025-26 already includes what councils spend, counted once, by two routes. £36.9bn is in the budget of the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government's local government department (central grants to councils), and £65.6bn is 'locally financed expenditure' (council spending paid for from council tax, retained business rates and fees). English councils' net current expenditure is £117bn (292 of 317 councils report 2025-26, the rest an earlier year), so council spending is largely inside the national total, and adding it to the total would count it twice.

notes: Other departments also pass grants to councils inside their own totals (for example Education for schools and Health for public health); the amounts are not separated in the Treasury tables we hold, so the route through departments is only partly visible here.

The Treasury table is for the whole UK public sector and includes the devolved governments' own spending; the council figure is England only. The two are not the same population of spending: they overlap, they do not add.
